name: Porcelain Green
lede: Porcelain Green is a muted, blue-leaning teal named for the glaze colors of Chinese porcelain, one of Ridgway's 1912 color standards.

sections.title: A glaze color, standardized
sections.body:
The name points to the teal and celadon-toned glazes used on Chinese porcelain, a color family potters had refined for centuries before Ridgway fixed one step of it as a naturalist's standard [1]. This shade is plate XXXIII, hue 39'', tone i, of Ridgway's 1912 color standards, read from a scan of an aged plate [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS system lists the same area as block 144, "light green," about 7.2 units from this exact shade, a wider gap than most of Ridgway's names show against their ISCC-NBS match [1]. Its Munsell notation is 6.2BG 5.1/3.8 [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[mint-turquoise]], [[wintergreen-dream]], [[jasper-green]] and [[dusty-teal]], at 2.8, 3.6, 4 and 5.3 ΔE [1]. Which porcelain tradition or glaze the name was drawn from is undocumented in the books we hold [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, this teal appears in 103, about 0.43 percent, rarer than 51 percent of our named colors [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 11 of 1,674 paintings, at 3.1 times the expected rate, and it is most over-represented in paintings from France, at 2.3 times the expected rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 42 percent of its matched paintings, rather than a light or an accent [2].

The earliest match is a 1445 panel by Domenico Veneziano, over four and a half centuries before Ridgway's 1912 name, so that early hit is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a trace of porcelain glaze, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. In printed English the word itself peaks in the 1870s, decades before Ridgway's 1912 standard, which suggests the color concept predates the formal name [2].
